query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy is primarily governed by the evolution of a passivating surface oxide layer enriched in Ti and Cr. In oxidizing atmospheres, this protective oxide initially forms on the fcc matrix to inhibit further oxygen ingress but later cracks or spalls due to elemental depletion, leading to accelerated matrix embrittlement and degradation. Conversely, in reducing atmospheres, the oxide film is less stable or does not fully develop, resulting in a different degradation pathway such as enhanced internal oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibiting a uniform face-centered cubic matrix with optimal strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to controlled elevated-temperature treatments under defined oxidizing (controlled oxygen partial pressure air) and reducing (hydrogen- or CO-enriched) gas environments.
generation.conditions: Temperatures in the range of 600–900 °C; exposure durations on the order of 100 hours; controlled gas compositions to distinctly simulate oxidizing versus reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, integrity, and eventual breakdown (e.g., cracking or spallation) of a thin, Ti- and Cr-enriched oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier for oxygen and modulates the elemental depletion of the underlying fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, rapid formation of a mixed TiO2/Cr2O3 oxide layer initially slows further oxidation; however, prolonged exposure leads to the breakdown of this layer and depletion of key alloying elements from the adjacent matrix, compromising mechanical integrity. Under reducing conditions, the oxide layer is either not fully established or is chemically reduced, leading to a more uniform internal oxidation that does not provide the initial protective effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-fabricated baseline, samples exposed in oxidizing atmospheres will first show a modest weight gain due to protective oxide formation, followed by accelerated losses in performance as the oxide scale deteriorates and causes localized elemental depletion. In contrast, samples exposed in reducing atmospheres will exhibit a different or lower rate of oxide development, with degradation marked by diffuse internal oxidation rather than oxide scale spallation.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the intact fcc microstructure and mechanical performance (strength and fatigue properties) of the as-fabricated additively manufactured alloy before any high-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to operate within moderate high-temperature exposures (600–900 °C) over durations up to around 100 hours. Under conditions significantly outside these bounds (e.g., very short exposures or extreme temperatures causing complete oxide melting), different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the roles of Ti and Cr in forming protective oxides are supported by analogous studies, the exact kinetics of oxidation, scale breakdown, and the relative contributions of each element remain uncertain. The possible influence of additive manufacturing microstructural heterogeneities on these processes is also not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples from the same batch of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and expose them at a set temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for 100 hours in two distinct environments: one with controlled oxidizing conditions (air with fixed oxygen partial pressure) and one with reducing conditions (a hydrogen- or CO-rich atmosphere). After exposure, assess weight change kinetics, microstructural alterations (via SEM/TEM and EDX mapping), phase evolution (using XRD), and mechanical properties (tensile or fatigue testing).
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging for the presence, morphology, and spallation of the oxide scale
EDX mapping to quantify Ti and Cr concentrations near the surface versus the bulk
XRD analysis to determine the phase composition of oxide layers
Mechanical testing (tensile/fatigue) to quantify degradation in performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under oxidizing conditions, the alloy does not show initial formation followed by breakdown of a Ti/Cr-rich oxide scale and corresponding localized depletion in the underlying matrix (or if reducing conditions yield a similar degradation profile as oxidizing exposures), then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
